🖼️ Framing Our Work

One way to cultivate literacy routines in our classrooms is to integrate routine writing.

By incorporating regular low-stakes, high-impact writing invitations, we can help young writers develop the skills to express their ideas, reflect on their experiences, and engage with the complexities of literacy—whether exploring texts, sharing personal stories, or responding to diverse perspectives.

Equally important, these routines empower students to see themselves as thinkers, readers, and writers who can participate meaningfully in the world around them. Finally, providing students with regular routines of reading and writing contributes to creating a classroom community of writers.

📝What to Expect

In this module, you will:

✅Explore the value of daily, low-stakes writing for student growth and agency.

✅Learn how to set up and use Writer’s Notebooks as spaces for practice and exploration.

✅Try out Quicklists to help students generate a range of writing topics.

✅Practice Writing Sprints to build stamina and fluency.

✅Share your own quicklist and reflections in the Everyday Sparks discussion, and connect with other teachers about how these practices might work in your classroom.

✅Earn the Everyday Sparks microcredential by reflecting with your facilitator on how you will adapt these strategies for your own students, including sharing a draft or example from your classroom.

🧭 Explore and Learn

The notion of finding time to include daily writing in an already packed curriculum seems overwhelming and perhaps impossible. And it is—if we think that this writing is separate from what we want writers to do in our classroom, if we think of this writing as discrete activities unattached to the work we are already doing as readers and writers.

But what if we open the possibilities? What if daily writing is connected to what students are already doing, capitalizes on the habits of readers and writers, and connects to the big picture of who our writers are? What if this daily writing is recursive, building on skills and returning to work already being done? Or maybe the writing is generative, acting as seeds for work to come.

In her piece "Hey Matt! There's a Reason We Write Like Every Day!" Molly Toussant, with one of her students as the audience, writes the following about her belief about the importance of practice for writers:

"We write every day for a reason. Learning how to write effectively takes a lot of practice. Matt, you play soccer, and knowing Mr. Viseur, your coach, I know you practice a lot. And it pays off, too—what did you win your last game by? Four, five goals? Writing is the same way. The more you practice writing, the better you’ll get. . .

At parent-teacher conferences this last year, your mom asked me, 'Why so much writing?' Writing is hard work—just like playing an instrument is hard work. Once when I heard one of my other favorite authors, Katie Wood Ray, speak about writing, she said, 'I write in my writer’s notebook throughout the day—I try things out: I jot down ideas and questions; I write descriptions and transcribe overheard conversations; I compose short poems and short story ideas; I copy down neat quotes I read in airplane magazines and on billboards.' As writers, we are not taking each piece we write to a final, polished piece—just as not every song played by a pianist is a recital or concert performance. But we try many things out in our writer’s notebooks, practicing before we select pieces to polish and share with others. The more we try out, the better we perform when it counts, the more we develop the ability to write with ease and craft and within conventional standards."

Regular low-stakes, high-impact writing invitations engage students and help build their skills as writers. Additionally, these routine practices foster student agency when we invite them to engage in conversations about topics that matter in their lives.

Keeping a Writer's Notebook

The Writer’s Notebook is a powerful tool for cultivating literacy routines, serving as both a space for exploration and a practice in consistency. Whether digital or hard-copy, the notebook becomes a writer’s personal workshop—a place to capture ideas, experiment with language, reflect on experiences, and respond to the world.

In a hard-copy Writer’s Notebook, students can engage with the tactile act of writing, adding sketches, annotations, and visual elements that bring their thinking to life. Digital notebooks, on the other hand, offer flexibility and accessibility, allowing for multimedia elements like links, images, and collaborative interactions.

By incorporating Writer’s Notebooks into daily or weekly routines, we encourage students to practice regularly, fostering habits of observation, reflection, and idea generation. Over time, these habits build confidence, fluency, and a deeper connection to their identity as writers.

But what to write about? Read on and explore some easy entry activities for engaging students in routine writing.

Quicklists

The first step in engaging students in routine writing is to help them find topics to write about. One way to find topics to write about is by creating a quicklist. We want to give student writers choices, but saying, “write about anything you want” without supporting them is often no choice at all. This strategy gives students a structure for generating a list of potential topics that they can return to again and again.

To create a quicklist, have students number from 1 to 10 in their notebooks. Share each prompt and have students quickly jot down their responses.

You can create quicklist prompts for a range of writing tasks and purposes. For example, to help students come up with topics for a personal narrative or reflective writing, you might use quicklist prompts like the ones below.

Personal Narrative Quicklist

  • 1-2 Two events from your life that have shaped who you are 

  • 3-4 Two vivid memories from your life

  • 5-6 Two experiences you have had that you are still trying to figure out

  • 7-8 Two memories that make you laugh

  • 9-10 Two times when you changed your mind about something

  • 11 One other life event, moment, or experience you are thinking about right now

Or, you might create a quicklist to help students identify argument topics that are relevant to their daily life.

Argument Quicklist

  • 1–2 List two things you did yesterday

  • 3–4 Two things you like that others might not

  • 5–6 Two conversations you have had recently (in-person or text/social media)

  • 7–8 Two things you don’t like that others do

  • 9-10 Two things you don’t think you could live without

  • 11 One other topic you are thinking about right now

Students return to the list and code it using an A for every topic that lends itself to an argument. These quicklist prompts can be adapted and changed throughout the year to discover more arguments.

Quicklist by Ulysses Cirilo, fourth grade teacher in Chicago

From here, writers have a ready-made list of argument topics. Students can return to this list for daily short writing, to practice specific argument skills like finding evidence or writing claims, or for longer self-selected research projects.

Note that the quicklist strategy, created by Gretchen Bernabei, is designed to generate a bunch of possible topics. It is meant to be done quickly and it might be helpful to let students know there is no wrong answer; the idea is to get down as many ideas as possible. If they can't think of an item, it is fine to just skip it and move on. They can always come back later to add additional items.

Writing Sprints

Writing sprints are short, focused bursts of writing designed to help students build writing stamina and confidence. After generating ideas—such as through quicklists—invite students to choose one or more topics and give them a set amount of time (often 3-5 minutes per topic). The idea is to write continuously on the topic without stopping to edit or overthink. The emphasis is on getting words down quickly, following their ideas wherever they lead. Writing sprints create momentum, lower the stakes of drafting, and help students discover that they have more to say than they might have realized at first.

Here is an example of a writing sprint process you might use to follow up on the topics students generated in a quicklist:

  1. Turn to a clean sheet of paper in your Writer's Notebook and write #1 on the top line.

  2. Choose one topic from your quicklist you want to write more about and write the topic next to #1.

  3. When I say start, begin writing as much as you can about your chosen topic. We will write for 3 minutes.

  4. When I say stop, write an ellipse (...) to note where your writing ended.

  5. Leave a few lines and repeat steps 1-4 for two more topics.

  6. Save your writing in your Writer's Notebook to return to later.

💬 Try and Share

Your turn! In your own Writer's Notebook, number from 1-10 and try out one of the quicklist options above (personal narrative or argument). Once you have generated a list of topics, try out writing 2-3 writing sprints using topics of your choice from your quicklist.

Then, take a picture of your quicklist and share it in the Everyday Sparks discussion, along with your reflections:

  • What was this process like for you? What potential topics did you come up with? Was anything surprising?

  • What ideas do you have for using or adapting this process with your students?

Remember that the discussions are a way for you to engage with other teachers in our community around the topics in the modules. Be sure to take a few minutes to respond to the posts from others in the discussion!
